title: Install a diesel air (parking) heater
summary: A diesel air heater burns about a tenth to half a litre of diesel an hour on the common 2–4 kW sizes and runs off a 12 V battery, heating a van, cabin, shed or boat with no exhaust in the room, as long as its combustion air and exhaust are both piped outside and sealed. A leaking or badly placed exhaust is what poisons people; a hot exhaust pipe against wood or plastic is what burns them out.

materials.item: Diesel air heater with its own metering pump, harness, controller, intake pipe, exhaust pipe and silencer
Fuel line of the size supplied (Webasto: 2 mm inside, nylon PA11 or PA12) with short rubber joiners and clips
Separate fuel tank, or a standpipe for the top of the vehicle tank
Steel exhaust pipe: rigid steel at least 1 mm wall, or alloyed-steel flex
Heat-proof sleeve or insulation where the exhaust passes through a floor or wall
Heater gasket or mounting plate seal (new, never reused)
Fuse and weatherproof holder, rating as the maker shows: 15 A (Webasto Air Top 2000 STC, 12 V), 20 A (Espar Airtronic D2, 12 V), 25 A (Autoterm diagrams)
Power cable straight to the battery
12 V battery able to supply the glow-plug start
Warm-air duct rated for at least 130 °C (266 °F); Espar asks for 149 °C (300 °F)

steps.text: Choose the spot: a flat, solid floor inside the space, or under it if the heater is protected from splash and road spray. Keep the heater and its exhaust at least 5 cm (2 in) from anything that burns or softens with heat (Espar's figure for the D2/D4; if your heater's own manual or label says more, use that). Leave room around the air inlet and outlet (Autoterm wants 5 cm at the inlet and 15 cm at the outlet on its AIR-2D and 4D). Keep clothing, sheets, paper, gas pipes and fuel tanks away from it, and never drape anything over it or in front of its inlet or outlet (Espar D2/D4, Autoterm Air).

Plan the three outside connections before drilling: combustion-air intake, exhaust and fuel line all end outside the heated space (Espar D2/D4). Put the exhaust where its fumes cannot come back in through a door, window, vent or the heater's own warm-air inlet, and at least 20–30 cm from the combustion-air intake (Webasto AT2000, Autoterm Air, Espar D2/D4).
steps.warn: An exhaust that ends under a door, beside a window or where snow drifts can block it will fill the space with carbon monoxide.

steps.text: Look under the floor before you drill, then cut the mounting hole and fit the heater on its gasket or mounting plate. The seal must be airtight, and a new one is needed every time the heater is refitted (Espar D2/D4, Webasto AT2000).
steps.warn: This seal keeps the exhaust side away from your air. Fit a new one every time, and don't overtighten a mounting plate: it warps (Webasto AT2000).

steps.text: Fit the exhaust: steel only, no longer than about 2 m, sloping down away from the heater or with a 4 mm drain hole at its lowest point, the outlet pointing down at about 90° and placed where snow, mud and splash can't block it (Webasto AT2000, Autoterm Air, Espar D2/D4). Seal every joint (Autoterm Air).
steps.warn: The exhaust runs up to 500 °C (Autoterm Air). Where it passes through a floor or wall it needs extra heat insulation, such as a heat-proof sleeve (Autoterm Air). Any part directly below a fuel tank needs 10 cm clear or a heat shield (Webasto AT2000).

steps.text: Fit the combustion-air intake: drawn from outside, never from where people are, from a cool spot that dirt, splash and snow can't clog, not facing the direction of travel, with its opening pointing down or a small drain hole at the low point (Webasto AT2000, Autoterm Air, Espar D2/D4).

Take fuel from a separate tank, or from a standpipe through the top of the vehicle tank, never its side (Autoterm Air). Never tap the engine's fuel filter, high-pressure line or return line (Autoterm Air). Use a metal tank fitting (Webasto AT2000) and keep the pickup end 10–15 mm above the tank bottom (Autoterm Air). Fitting a standpipe means opening a fuel tank: use a spare sender-gauge plate or an existing plug in the tank top where there is one (Espar D2/D4); if you must drill, Autoterm says to take the precautions for work on a tank full of fuel (Autoterm Air).
steps.warn: Switch the heater off while any tank on the vehicle is being filled (Espar D2/D4). A drill, a spark or heat on a tank that holds or has held petrol can set off its vapour: fit the standpipe cold, with no flame or grinder nearby.

steps.text: Mount the metering pump on its rubber mount, close to the tank, in a cool place away from exhaust heat, tilted slightly upward toward its outlet so air bubbles pass through it (Autoterm Air, Espar D2/D4). Never wire it to a steady 12 V: it runs on pulses from the heater (Autoterm Air).

Run the fuel line with the maker's tubing, as short as possible, butt-jointed inside the rubber joiners with no gap, rising gently to the heater, clipped against sagging and at least 10 cm (4 in) from the exhaust (the 10 cm is from Webasto's checklist; Autoterm says only no contact with hot objects). Keep it out of the passenger cabin, and keep the heater's 12 V wiring away from the fuel line and the exhaust (Autoterm Air). Webasto's limits: intake side 5 m, pressure side 10 m, 12 m in total (Webasto AT2000).

Wire the power straight to the battery with the fuse within about 35 cm (14 in) of it: 15 A for a 12 V Webasto Air Top 2000 STC, 20 A for a 12 V Espar Airtronic D2, and 25 A in Autoterm's wiring diagrams (Webasto AT2000, Espar D2/D4, Autoterm Air). Fit the fuse last, after every other connection is made (Espar D2/D4), and never use a different rating or a bit of wire in place of a fuse (Autoterm Air). A cigarette-lighter socket is not good enough for the start current (Webasto AT2000).

Route the warm-air duct in material that takes at least 130 °C (266 °F), aim the outlet at least 20 cm (8 in) from anyone, and don't let hot outlet air short-circuit back to the inlet (Webasto AT2000). Espar asks for ducts and outlets that take at least 300 °F (149 °C) on its D2/D4, so use that if you can (Espar D2/D4). The outlet and duct get hot enough to burn: keep infants, sleeping or sedated people and bedding away from them, and never cover the inlet or outlet (Webasto AT2000, Autoterm Air).

Put a battery CO alarm in the heated space before the first run (safety_carbon_monoxide). Fit fresh batteries, check the date on the back, and test it: the test button checks the horn and electronics, not the sensor (First Alert test). Read the temperature range on the label too, because a freezing van can sit below it, and treat a headache or nausea as CO whatever the alarm says.

Put a smoke alarm and a fire extinguisher where people sleep (Autoterm requires an extinguisher in a vehicle fitted with its heater, Autoterm Air), and keep a window or door that opens and is clear of snow and gear.

First start: the fuel line may need several start attempts or priming to fill. Expect a smell for the first few hours, so keep the space ventilated; Autoterm has the first session run on maximum for about 2 hours (Autoterm Air). With it running, walk round outside: the exhaust should leave only from the outlet, and nothing should smell of fumes inside.
steps.warn: Any exhaust smell, soot at a joint or a CO alarm: switch off, ventilate, and find the leak before running it again.

steps.text: Run it at least 20 minutes once a month, even in summer; Autoterm says on full power (Espar D2/D4, Autoterm Air).

notes:
## How it works
A diesel air heater has two separate air paths. A small blower pulls outside air into a combustion chamber, where a glow pin lights diesel dosed in by a clicking metering pump; the exhaust leaves through its own pipe. A second blower pushes room air over the outside of the heat exchanger and back into the room (Espar D2/D4, Autoterm Air). As long as the gasket, heat exchanger and exhaust joints are sound, no exhaust enters the room. Webasto warns that bad installation or repair can cause fire or deadly carbon monoxide leakage (Webasto AT2000), which is why a CO alarm goes in with it.

## Numbers from the makers
| Heater | Heat | Fuel | 12 V draw |
|---|---|---|---|
| Espar Airtronic D2 | 0.85–2.2 kW | 0.10–0.28 L/h | 8.3 A starting, 0.7–2.8 A running |
| Espar Airtronic D4 | 1.0–4.0 kW | 0.13–0.51 L/h | 8.3 A starting, 0.6–3.3 A running |
| Webasto Air Top 2000 STC D | 0.9–2.0 kW | 0.12–0.24 L/h | 75 W starting, 14–29 W running |
| Autoterm AIR-2D | 0.8–2.0 kW | 0.10–0.24 L/h | 10–29 W running |

From Espar D2/D4, Webasto AT2000 and Autoterm Air. The start draw is the glow pin heating up for about a minute before fuel flows (Espar D2/D4). A D2 that runs mostly on medium (1.0 A) for 12 hours takes about 12 Ah from the battery. Each start and stop adds roughly 0.3–0.4 Ah: up to 8.3 A through about 60 s of preheat, about 60 s more after the flame lights, and a 40 s after-glow at shutdown (worked from Espar D2/D4). Espar's heaters shut down below 10.5 V (Espar D2/D4) and Webasto wants the battery at 12.2 V or more before the first start (Webasto AT2000): a tired battery gives failed starts, not heat. See [power budget](#guides/reference_power_budget).

## Installation rules that matter most
| What | Rule | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Combustion air | From outside, never from where people are | Webasto AT2000, Espar D2/D4 |
| Exhaust outlet | Away from doors, windows, vents and the warm-air inlet; not into the wind of travel; clear of snow and mud | Webasto AT2000, Espar D2/D4, Autoterm Air |
| Intake to exhaust | At least 20 cm by Autoterm's figure, 30 cm by Espar's | Autoterm Air, Espar D2/D4 |
| Exhaust pipe | Steel, about 2 m maximum, drained, outlet down at 90° ± 10° | Webasto AT2000, Espar D2/D4 |
| Exhaust through floor or wall | Extra heat insulation at the pass-through | Autoterm Air |
| Heat clearance | 5 cm (2 in) from flammable or heat-sensitive material | Espar D2/D4 |
| Fuel line | Maker's size, short, rising to the heater, 10 cm from exhaust | Webasto AT2000 |
| Metering pump | Near the tank, cool, slightly tilted up toward its outlet | Autoterm Air, Espar D2/D4 |
| Power | Direct to battery, fused close to it | Webasto AT2000, Espar D2/D4 |

The three manuals here cover vehicles and boats; none describes a cabin, shed or workshop. If you fit one in a building, keep every rule above and treat the exhaust as a pipe that reaches 500 °C (Autoterm Air): never pass it bare through a wooden wall or floor, but through a pass-through made for hot flues, with an air gap or non-combustible insulation, as in [installing a stove](#guides/build_stove_install). Both Webasto and Autoterm allow the heating air to be taken from outside instead of from the room, but Autoterm advises against it for safety: it loses heating capacity, uses more fuel and power, and carries a high risk of drawing exhaust gases (yours or another vehicle's) into the living space (Autoterm Air). Webasto wants heating air from a clean area that exhaust cannot reach (Webasto AT2000). Take room air back through the heater unless you can be sure its inlet stays well clear of its own exhaust.

## Where not to put one
- Not where flammable vapour, gas or lots of dust can collect. Espar says no enclosed areas with combustible fumes, Autoterm no places where flammable vapours, gases or large amounts of dust may form (Espar D2/D4, Autoterm Air). That rules out a garage or workshop holding petrol, solvents, propane or sawdust.
- Not in the engine compartment of a petrol-powered boat (Espar D2/D4).
- Not in a closed garage or bay unless its exhaust is piped outside (Espar D2/D4).
- Switch it off while refuelling or loading flammables (Espar D2/D4, Webasto AT2000).

## Carbon monoxide alarm
Many alarms are rated for 4.4–37.8 °C (40–100 °F) only and are not to be mounted where it is colder or hotter, so read the label before trusting one in a freezing van (First Alert CO710). First Alert says its alarm typically does not detect CO below 30 ppm and is built not to sound at a constant 30 ppm for 30 days, and says to replace the alarm 10 years after installation (First Alert CO710). So a headache, nausea or dizziness is a reason to open up and get out, alarm or not.

## Fuel
- **Diesel.** Autoterm says EN 590 diesel suited to the temperature; Espar says fuel suitable for the climate; Webasto allows diesel or North American heating oil of normal quality in its diesel model (Autoterm Air, Espar D2/D4, Webasto AT2000).
- **Switching to winter fuel:** run the heater about 15 minutes so the new fuel fills the line and pump (Webasto AT2000).
- **Biodiesel:** the Espar D2 is not certified for it beyond blends of about 10 %; Autoterm says no biofuel; the Webasto Air Top 2000 STC is licensed for EN 14214 biodiesel (Espar D2/D4, Autoterm Air, Webasto AT2000).
- **Never:** used engine oil blended into the diesel (Espar D2/D4). Petrol only in heaters built for it, such as Webasto's separate 'B' gasoline model (Webasto AT2000); never in a diesel heater ([fuel](#browse/hazards/fuel)).
- **Other fuels:** Autoterm says to use only EN 590 diesel in its heaters (Autoterm Air). Webasto's diesel model takes diesel or heating oil of normal North American quality, and only its separate 'B' model is built for petrol (Webasto AT2000).
- **Old fuel:** with a separate tank, change the fuel at least once a season and rinse out the sediment before winter, or the pump clogs and the burner soots up (Autoterm Air).

## Smoke and carbon
Espar lists the causes of a heater that smokes and carbons up: blocked exhaust, blocked combustion-air intake, exhaust drawn back into the intake, short on-off cycling, fuel-system faults and wrong pump delivery (Espar D2/D4). Autoterm's exhaust end-shield is needed for stable running at low settings (Autoterm Air). Espar's maintenance list: pull the glow pin and its screen and clean off carbon, check intake and exhaust for blockage, and run the heater 20 minutes a month (Espar D2/D4). Autoterm adds a yearly check of fuel hoses, exhaust seals and corrosion (Autoterm Air).

## Altitude and cold
The Espar D2 heats without limits up to 1,500 m; above that only for short spells unless the fuel delivery is adjusted (Espar D2/D4). It is rated for air down to −40 °C (Espar D2/D4); Autoterm's air heaters to −45 °C (Autoterm Air).

## Cheap units
UK product-safety reports on several cheap Chinese-made diesel parking heaters (all Vevor models) found them sold with missing or inadequate installation instructions and warnings, including nothing telling the buyer to keep the exhaust away from combustible material, so users could fit them in ways that leak poisonous exhaust or start fires; the imports were turned back at the border (OPSS Vevor 2302-0090, OPSS Vevor 2212-0139, OPSS Vevor 2212-0144). If yours came with thin instructions, install it to the Webasto and Espar rules above, and check every exhaust joint and the mounting gasket before trusting it in a closed space.
